  "text": "In spring the harbour office needed a new shelf. The old one had sagged beneath the tide books until its middle rested on the radiator.

Maren took the books down. Behind them lay a shopping list in her mother's hand.

Tea. Soap. Two pears.

Nothing on the back.

She sat with it while the carpenter measured the wall. He asked whether she wanted the new shelf higher. She said the same height would do.

For years she had looked for something Agnes might have left her. An explanation folded into a ledger. A warning beneath a drawer. Now there were two pears, and she could not remember whether her mother had liked them hard or soft.

She put the list in her pocket.

That evening Erris met her outside the shop. The girl had grown enough that her coat sleeves no longer reached her wrists.

"What time is it?"

"Half past five."

Erris looked at the bag in Maren's hand.

"Those aren't ripe."

"They will be."

At home Maren set the pears on the kitchen sill. She cooked, washed up, and read until it was time to leave. Before going out she moved one pear away from the cold glass.

The climb was no easier for the milder weather. She stopped at the landing and caught her breath. Then she went on.

Afterward she came home by the harbour. A boat knocked gently against its fenders.

In the kitchen she left the shopping list beside the fruit. She would not put it in the log.

She went upstairs to bed."

  "text": "Four days later, one pear softened at the stem. The other remained hard, its skin yellowing around a small dark mark.

Maren ate the ripe one standing at the sink. Juice ran beneath her weddingless finger and into her cuff. She had fetched no plate. Outside, someone was dragging a chain across the quay, stopping whenever she thought the noise had finished.

She wrapped the second pear in her mother's list and took it to the office.

Erris came at noon to return a ruler. She had borrowed it in February, for something she no longer remembered.

"Is that for me?"

Maren unfolded the paper.

"Cut round the bad bit."

There was a knife in the desk. Erris divided the pear unevenly and gave Maren the smaller piece. They ate beside the new shelf, which smelled of sawn wood whenever the radiator warmed.

Through the window Maren could see the lighthouse. A gull stood on its railing. From here the bird seemed larger than the door through which she entered every evening.

Erris asked whether she could come up sometime.

Maren wiped the knife, slowly, with a corner of the paper. She stopped when she saw what she was using.

"Tomorrow," she said. "If it's dry."

After the girl left, Maren laid the list on the radiator. The damp patch spread through Soap, then dried to a faint translucence.

At closing time she put it in the drawer with the ruler and the knife.

She checked the next morning's tide. Then, on a separate scrap, she wrote herself a reminder to bring the smaller torch."

  "text": "It was not dry, but Erris came anyway, with her hair tucked into the neck of her coat.

Maren gave her the smaller torch. On the stairs its beam travelled ahead of them, catching old screw holes and the pale undersides of the treads. Twice the girl stopped without saying why. Twice Maren waited.

At the top, rain had found its usual place beneath the eastern window. Maren moved the bucket half an inch. The next drop struck its bottom with a sound that seemed too large for the room.

"Does the light still work?"

"No."

Erris considered the covered machinery.

"Could it?"

Maren had brought the log upstairs under her coat. She laid it on the narrow table and pressed flat a page that had curled in the damp.

"Hold that here," she said.

The girl aimed the torch while Maren entered the time, the weather, the water beneath the window. Her handwriting looked unfamiliar in the small white circle. She left room below it.

Outside, the harbour disappeared by degrees. First the far wall, then the boats, then the office where the drawer held the knife and the list. The bell buoy remained audible, though neither of them could have pointed to it.

Erris asked if they should go down.

"In a minute."

Maren checked the window latch. When she turned back, the girl was still holding the light over the open book, carefully, as though Maren had more to write.

She took the pen out again and entered the girl's name beside her own."
